title: Position: Stop Automating Peer Review Without Rigorous Evaluation
claim: Machine-generated outputs are more homogeneous with one another than human-influenced ones, revealing a hidden loss of diversity.
layout: single panel, density plot, two overlaid curves, dashed mean lines, legend top-right
description: A single kernel density plot with InterSim (pairwise review similarity) on the x-axis from 0 to 1 and Density on the y-axis up to about 6. Two nearly overlapping bell curves are drawn. A coral-red curve is for fully AI-generated reviews. A teal curve is for other reviews (AI-edited plus human). Both are translucent filled and peak near 0.45 to 0.5. Vertical dashed lines mark each group's mean. The red mean is 0.486 and sits slightly right of the teal mean of 0.467. A legend in the top-right lists the groups and the mean values. The eye goes first to the two overlapping peaks and the small rightward shift of the red curve. Light gridlines and bold axis labels keep the look clean.
caption: The AI reviewer hivemind effect in ICLR 2026 reviews. Distribution of pairwise inter-paper review similarity (In- terSim) for fully AI-generated reviews versus all other reviews (human-written and AI-assisted). Fully AI-generated reviews show significantly higher within-group similarity (mean = 0.486) compared to other reviews (mean = 0.467; t = 3218, p < 0.0001, Cohen’s d = 0.29). Data: 75,800 ICLR 2026 reviews with AI- generation labels from Emi (2025).
abstract: Large language models offer a tempting solution to address the peer review crisis. This position paper argues that today's AI systems should not be used to produce paper reviews. We ground this position in an empirical comparison of human- versus AI-generated ICLR 2026 reviews and an evaluation of the effect of automated paper rewriting on different AI reviewers. We identify two critical issues: 1) AI reviewers exhibit a hivemind effect of excessive agreement within and across papers that reduces perspective diversity. 2) AI review scores are trivially gameable through paper laundering: prompting an LLM to rewrite a paper could significantly increase the scores from AI reviewers, demonstrating that LLM reviewers are easy to game through stylistic changes rather than scientific results. However, non-gameability and review diversity are necessary but not sufficient conditions for automation. We argue that addressing the peer review crisis requires a science of peer review automation -- not general-purpose LLMs deployed without rigorous evaluation.
